html_source:
In brief

As Simon Dedalus begins the first bars of "M'appari," Bloom signals to the waiter to leave the door ajar, wishing to hear the gorgeous singing voice. As it floats through the room he removes a rubber band from a packet of papers and begins to wind it absently around his fingers. These actions duplicate the central action of Homer's episode: Odysseus being tied to his ship's mast with ropes so that he can listen to the sirens' song. The echoes of this incident resound for many subsequent paragraphs as Bloom, fingering the knotted strings, contemplates the song's message of sexual attraction and loss. The image of a bound man captures his take on that message: what we find "alluring" is a "lure," a potentially fatal trap.

At more length

"Through the hush of air a voice sang to them, low" (the aria begins on a low A, and the dynamic is piano), Lionel telling of the time when first he saw his Martha. Bloom and Richie Goulding find music "touching their still ears with words, still hearts of their each his remembered lives. Good, good to hear: sorrow from them each seemed to from both depart when first they heard. When first they saw, lost Richie Poldy, mercy of beauty, heard from a person wouldn't expect it in the least, her first merciful lovesoft oftloved word." Reliving that surprising feeling of being loved by Molly, Bloom performs his Odyssean action: "Bloom unwound slowly the elastic band of his packet. [...] Bloom wound a skein round four forkfingers, stretched it, relaxed, and wound it round his troubled double, fourfold, in octave, gyved them fast." He forms a cat's cradle with his "octave" of eight fingers. Calling them "gyved"—fettered, shackled—sounds threatening, but if a Homeric correspondence is intended Bloom's action must be viewed as in some way protecting him from a threat.

Threatening thoughts follow immediately, as Bloom thinks of operatic tenors seducing scores of women, of his own Martha's desire to adulterously "meet," of female beauty making male heads "swirl," of a brass bed's "Jingle all delighted," and on and on. His reflections on adultery conclude with the sentence, "Hands felt for the opulent"—a literary anticipation of Boylan entering the house and caressing Molly's breasts. After these ominous reflections, the song enters a new emotional register, "loud, full, shining, proud," and then a place of tender sexual longing: "Tenderness it welled: slow, swelling. Full it throbbed. That's the chat. Ha, give! Take! Throb, a throb, a pulsing proud erect." Seemingly in response to all these emotional triggers, Bloom's fingers play with the knots binding them: "Bloom looped, unlooped, noded, disnoded." People familiar with cat's cradles will recognize the physical actions he performs, but no doubt they also image mental actions. Homer's hero orders his men to free him but "Eurylochus and Perimedes stood / and tied me even tighter, with more knots" (12.195-6). The theme of being protected from danger persists.

Having been aroused to sexual excitement, Bloom thinks of writing Martha Clifford and finds binding ropes there too: "Martha it is. Coincidence. Just going to write. Lionel's song. Lovely name you have. Can't write. Accept my little pres. Play on her heartstrings pursestrings too." The song continues, and now its meditation on "How first he saw that form endearing" sends Bloom back to Molly again, and that "First night when first I saw her at Mat Dillon's in Terenure." The bright seductive details of this first meeting swirl through his mind, concluding with Molly's thanking him for turning the pages of her music: "First I saw. She thanked me. Why did she me? Fate. Spanishy eyes. [...] At me. Luring. Ah, alluring." This last thought, anticipated in the chapter's overture ("Ah, lure! Alluring"), captures Bloom's quandary. Molly is his alluring siren, and in every allurement there is a lure for the unwary, a sorrow lying in wait. "M'appari" strikes this concluding note: "Quitting all languor Lionel cried in grief, in cry of passion dominant to love to return with deepening yet with rising chords of harmony. In cry of lionel loneliness that she should know, must Martha feel. For only her he waited." Bloom too feels this lonely grief: "Alone. One love. One hope. One comfort me. Martha, chestnote, return!"

After the song ends, narrative attention drifts away from lonely Leopold and his gyved fingers, but they return in a kind of coda many paragraphs later: "Bloom ungyved his crisscrossed hands and with slack fingers plucked the slender catgut thong. He drew and plucked. It buzzed, it twanged." The magnificent music is gone now, replaced by a mere buzzing twang, but Bloom continues to meditate on its desolate theme: "Thou lost one. All songs on that theme. Yet more Bloom stretched his string. Cruel it seems. Let people get fond of each other: lure them on. Then tear asunder. Death. Explos. Knock on the head. Outtohelloutofthat. Human life." To love is to risk losing.

The scene painted in this part of Sirens bears some resemblance to the dismal scene in Lestrygonians when Bloom recalls happier days with Molly while watching a pair of copulating flies: "Stuck on the pane two flies buzzed, stuck. […] Me. And me now. / Stuck, the flies buzzed." But although Bloom's fingers are "gyved" in Sirens, the Homeric correspondence suggests that this is a defensive posture to ward off ruin. The cat's cradle images a state of mind more complex than mere dejection. Like Odysseus, Bloom hears Lionel's enrapturing sad song from a distance and is preserved.

John Hunt 2026
